meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Those who built the visionary companies wisely understood that it is better to understand who you are than where you are going, for where you are going will almost certainly change'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine: Jim Collins and Jerry Porras wrote it in the Introduction to the Paperback Edition of Built to Last (HarperBusiness, 1997).

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorName: Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras
answer.authorDates: Jim Collins b. 1958 · business researcher & author; co-author Jerry I. Porras
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in the “Introduction to the Paperback Edition” of Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies (HarperBusiness, 1st paperback ed., 1997), which Collins co-wrote with Jerry I. Porras. The original has an em dash where the popular version has a comma (“…than where you are going—for where you are going will almost certainly change”). The introduction was new to the paperback, so the line is not in the 1994 first edition.

source.heading: Where the line appears

docMeta.dd: Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies

source.excerpt: People cannot reliably predict where they are going and how their lives will unfold, especially in today’s unpredictable world. Those who built the visionary companies wisely understood that it is better to understand who you are than where you are going—for where you are going will almost certainly change. It is a lesson as relevant to our individual lives as to aspiring visionary companies.
trail: The Internet Archive’s catalog record for the 1997 HarperBusiness “1st pbk. ed.” notes that the “Paperback edition includes a new introduction and a new chapter by the authors” (Internet Archive ↗).
A full-text search of that scan returns the passage: “…you are going — for where you are going will almost certainly change. It is a lesson as…” (Internet Archive full-text search ↗).
Wikiquote’s sourced quotes for Jim Collins list the line under Built to Last, citing p. xx (Wikiquote ↗).

Collins and Porras had made the same point in their Harvard Business Review article “Building Your Company’s Vision” (HBR ↗). There it reads “more important to know who you are than where you are going” (reposted text ↗).
source.excerptNote: In the book this passage closes a discussion of readers who applied the book’s “preserve the core/stimulate progress” idea to their own lives. The next heading is “Ongoing Learning and Future Work.”

author.bio: James C. “Jim” Collins (born January 25, 1958, in Aurora, Colorado) studied at Stanford and joined the faculty of the Stanford Graduate School of Business in 1988. He wrote Built to Last (1994) with his Stanford colleague Jerry I. Porras, and later wrote Good to Great (2001), How the Mighty Fall (2009) and Great by Choice (2011, with Morten T. Hansen).

misattribution.heading: What the popular version gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The words are genuine. What the popular version gets wrong is the credit around them: it names one author when there were two, and it gives the wrong edition.

items.why: Built to Last is co-written by Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras (Wikipedia ↗). The paperback introduction is signed by both authors. Quote sites such as Quotewise credit “James C. Collins” alone (Quotewise ↗).

Quotewise dates the line to 1994, and Wikiquote files it under the book’s 1994 heading (Wikiquote ↗). But the passage sits in an introduction written for the paperback (Internet Archive ↗). That introduction opens by recalling that the authors shipped the final manuscript on March 14, 1994, and says “as we write this introduction to the paperback edition.” We searched the full text of the Internet Archive’s 1994 and 1995 scans of the book and did not find the passage.

A similar line, “more important to know who you are than where you are going,” comes from Collins and Porras’s 1996 Harvard Business Review article (reposted text ↗). A version of it also appears in the paperback’s new chapter, “Building the Vision.” It is the same authors restating the same idea, but it is a different sentence and should not be merged with this one.

misattribution.truthLine: It is genuine: Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras wrote it in the Introduction to the Paperback Edition of Built to Last (HarperBusiness, 1997) (Internet Archive ↗).

context.heading: Why the authors wrote it
lead: Built to Last argues that long-lasting companies keep a fixed “core ideology” while changing everything else. The book’s name for this is “preserve the core/stimulate progress.” In the new introduction for the paperback, Collins and Porras reported that many readers had applied that idea to their own lives and to questions of identity and renewal.

The sentence is their conclusion to that discussion. The founders of the visionary companies anchored on identity rather than on destination, and the authors say the same lesson applies to individuals.
context.pull: It is a lesson as relevant to our individual lives as to aspiring visionary companies.
